1080.bp: When you use chat bots or AI systems to recommend products, movies, or books, those systems learn from watching what you interact with—whether you click, like, or buy. The goal is to make recommendations so good that you actually want what they suggest. But unlike traditional recommenders that just score items, generative recommenders literally compose text descriptions of products, asking the system to *generate* what to show you next.
1080.wh: The hard part comes from the messy reality of user feedback. Some clicks mean 'I really want this,' others mean 'I was curious,' and some mean 'this was available when I had five seconds.' The same click from two people can mean opposite things. If you treat all feedback the same when tuning the recommender, you're asking it to learn from noise—contradictory signals that pull the system in different directions at once.
1080.ap: This team built a system that learns *confidence* for each piece of feedback, then adapts how hard it pushes the recommender based on that confidence. When the system is certain a user action means 'yes, recommend more like this,' it trains aggressively. When it's uncertain—say, a click that might just be accidental—it trains gently, accepting that the system won't learn cleanly from that signal. They also add a brake that prevents the recommender from forgetting to assign decent probabilities to the items you marked as preferred.
1080.ww: This works because it mirrors how a good teacher acts: hammering home the lessons you're sure about, and staying flexible on ambiguous cases. By letting the system express how confident it is in each feedback signal, and then using that confidence to control training intensity, you avoid the trap of overfitting to random clicks. The brake on probability collapse prevents the recommender from gaming the system by just lowering all scores indiscriminately.
1080.po: On real recommendation datasets, this approach beats older methods by improving how often users click on the top suggestions. The system learns which signals truly matter and trains more stable, personalized recommenders that don't chase every noisy click equally.

1081.bp: When you search Google or browse a shopping site, you see a ranked list of results. But that ranking is affected by two very different things: how relevant each result actually is *and* where it sits on the page. Results at the top get clicked more simply because they're there, even if something lower down would have been more helpful. Teasing apart these two effects is crucial for making search better.
1081.wh: Every method today assumes there's *one* true answer: item X is relevant or not relevant, position Y has a certain bias. But in reality, you never see the truth directly—you only see clicks, which mingle relevance and position together. And here's the real problem: you don't know how uncertain you should be in your answer. Maybe the click pattern you see today will look completely different next week, or on a different device. Traditional methods give you a single number—'this item is 80% relevant'—but they hide their doubt.
1081.ap: These researchers built a system that outputs not single numbers but *probability distributions*—essentially, a range of plausible answers with varying confidence. Instead of saying 'the item is relevant,' it says 'this distribution of relevance-values best describes what we know, given the data we've seen.' The system learns these distributions using a deep neural network that takes item and position features and outputs a beta distribution for each factor (relevance and bias).
1081.ww: This captures something profound: past data can't tell you everything. A click might mean high relevance, or it might mean good positioning, or both, or neither. By outputting distributions, the system admits this uncertainty explicitly. On unseen data (like next week's searches), this honest uncertainty becomes an asset—you know which predictions to trust and which ones are guesses.
1081.po: The method successfully estimates how much you should trust each prediction of relevance and position bias, whereas standard approaches pretend certainty even when the data is ambiguous. This matters for ranking systems because it flags when to ask for more information rather than confidently giving a wrong answer.

1082.bp: Modern recommendation systems can use images and text together—not just collaborative signals like 'people who liked this also liked that.' A movie recommender might show you a poster, synopsis, and reviews all at once. But fusing all these sources is tricky: text and images need to be represented in compatible ways, and user-item interactions (what you clicked) can conflict with what the images and text suggest.
1082.wh: The core tension: collaborative signals (your clicks) and semantic signals (the visual and textual content) live in different worlds. A user might click a horror movie after browsing thrillers, but if the images show a peaceful forest, those signals contradict. Additionally, the connections between users and items (from clicks) can be noisy or sparse—you've only clicked a tiny fraction of items. And when merging multiple graphs (one for user-item clicks, another for item-item connections via images), it's unclear how to weight them or even if they should be treated separately.
1082.ap: The system builds multiple graph layers and learns to clean them up automatically. It starts with a user-item interaction graph (clicks and ratings) and a separate item-item graph built from shared visual and textual features. Instead of treating these edges as fixed, it iteratively *reweights* them during training, turning noisy connections down and strong ones up. Simultaneously, it aligns the semantic space (from images and text) with the collaborative space (from clicks) by enforcing that aligned concepts should predict each other, and applies a lightweight cleanup to remove redundant dimensions across views.
1082.ww: Reweighting edges dynamically works because the system learns which connections actually matter—users do click together for semantic reasons sometimes, and those signals amplify. By forcing the two representation spaces to align, you prevent the image-based view from contradicting the click-based view. Removing redundancy stabilizes learning because you're not training the same pattern twice in different coordinate systems.
1082.po: On Amazon product datasets, this multi-graph fusion beats simpler baselines by 7-8%, improving both ranking accuracy and recall—more relevant recommendations, and more of them. The system successfully disentangles meaningful semantic relationships from noisy clicks.

1083.bp: Mathematicians publish thousands of papers a year, and finding related work is hard because a paper on permutation groups might be deeply connected to a paper on computational topology, even though they use completely different vocabulary and never cite each other. A mathematician writes 'prove that X implies Y using the sandwich lemma,' while another writes 'the homotopy-theoretic dual shows that Z is a generalization of W.' Same ideas, different words—or subtly different ideas in the same domain. Recommending relevant papers means understanding these conceptual links.
1083.wh: Text-based similarity fails: two papers about the same proof technique might share almost no sentences. Citation networks fail: papers in different eras or fields rarely cite each other even if they're cousins. And relevance isn't one-dimensional—a paper might be related through 'uses the same algebraic structure,' 'extends the main theorem,' or 'applies the technique to a new domain.' These aspects of relatedness can conflict: a paper might extend the theorem but use a completely different proof structure.
1083.ap: The team built a dataset of expert-rated recommendations (GoldRiM, hand-labeled) and a larger automatic version (SilverRiM). Then they created a graph neural network that ingests three types of information at once: the text of abstracts, the citation network, and the author lineage (who trained whom, who collaborates). The network learns to weight these channels differently depending on which aspects of relatedness matter for the current recommendation task—essentially, it conditions its decisions on 'what kind of relation are we looking for?'
1083.ww: This works because mathematics is built on lineage, networks, and shared techniques that transcend text. By explicitly modeling authorship (who co-authored with whom, academic genealogy), the system captures intellectual influence that citations miss. By conditioning on aspects, it acknowledges that a paper can be related through multiple distinct mechanisms, and learns to weight them appropriately.
1083.po: On hand-labeled mathematical data, the system beats prior aspect-based recommenders on all measured aspects, and significantly outperforms pure text-based methods. The key insight is that mathematical relatedness is structural and genealogical, not just textual.

1084.bp: Modern recommenders use large language models (LLMs) to understand what items are about and to reason about good recommendations. But LLMs need short, crisp identifiers for items—product IDs, user tags, etc. The way you label an item dramatically changes how well the LLM can work with it. A bad identifier is confusing; a good one helps the LLM reason correctly.
1084.wh: Traditional identifiers (product names, catalog numbers) are inconsistent in length and mix semantic meaning with database artifacts. An LLM might struggle with 'Product-2847-Blue-XL-Refresh-2024' because it's verbose and mixes multiple concepts. Existing methods that assign short learned codes (like 'item_512') ignore what items are actually about—the LLM has to guess from context. And when you add new items or move to a different catalog, these learned codes don't transfer; you have to start from scratch.
1084.ap: The team built a graph neural network that encodes both collaborative signals (how users interact with items) and semantic signals (item features like category, price, description). The network produces compact, meaningful identifiers. They then cluster these representations using a tree-based hierarchy, where the depth of the tree controls the length of the final code. This is faster than old spectral clustering methods and allows quick updates as new items arrive, without retraining the whole system.
1084.ww: Fusing attributes and collaborative signals means the identifier captures both 'what is this item?' (from features) and 'who wants it?' (from user behavior). A hierarchical tree naturally produces short codes at the top levels (fast, general) and longer codes for fine-grained distinctions. This structure lets an LLM use the code as a meaningful abbreviation: 'Electronics/Audio/Headphones/Wireless/Premium' might become a compact token that the model recognizes semantically.
1084.po: Across five benchmark datasets, the method achieves strong ranking accuracy and generalizes well to new datasets without retraining. The identifiers are interpretable and compact, and the system scales efficiently for real-world catalogs with millions of items.

1085.bp: You ask an AI system 'What is the capital of France in an alternate reality where Napoleon won?' and it should use your question to override its training—preferring the alternate scenario over real history. But LLMs are biased toward facts they've seen millions of times in training. They often ignore your contextual facts and confidently answer based on their parametric knowledge: 'Paris,' not 'London' or whatever your alternate scenario specifies.
1085.wh: The problem is that LLMs encode world knowledge deeply and broadly. When you provide a fact that contradicts training data—'In this scenario, the capital moved'—the model's learned associations are so strong that they leak through. The model sees 'capital' and 'France' and fires the 'Paris' pattern regardless of your setup. Even reasoning models with long thinking chains fail here because reasoning happens after the prior knowledge has already biased the answer space.
1085.ap: The approach is elegant: find entities mentioned in both the context and the question, then replace them with generic labels that strip away real-world associations. 'Paris' becomes 'City‖1⟩' and 'France' becomes 'Country‖1⟩.' This preprocessing stage is entirely offline—you don't retrain the model. At test time, the system substitutes these abstract names into the prompt. After the model generates an answer using these neutral labels, you map them back to the real entities.
1085.ww: This works because you're removing the spurious associations while keeping the relational structure intact. The model sees 'City‖1⟩ is in Country‖1⟩' and reasons about that relationship without the baggage of 'Paris → tourist destination → fame → override?' The abstraction lets the model focus on structure: if the context says 'City‖1⟩ moved to City‖2⟩,' the model can follow that logic without fighting ingrained world knowledge.
1085.po: On counterfactual and knowledge-conflict benchmarks, this lightweight preprocessing beats even state-of-the-art reasoning models by up to 25% for medium models (0.5B–18B). It's fast, requires no retraining, and works across open and closed-source models.

1086.bp: Imagine a movie recommender trained to generate recommendations using an LLM. It learns to say 'try Inception, it's sci-fi and visually stunning.' But when a new movie arrives tomorrow (cold-start), the system has no training data for it and recommends nearly random garbage. The system can't handle dynamic catalogs where new items appear constantly.
1086.wh: Retraining the full model with new item data is prohibitively expensive and slow. In real systems, new items arrive hourly or minute-by-minute. The traditional response—collect interactions on new items, then retrain—creates weeks of lag. But there's a deeper issue: sequential recommendation data (the sequence of movies you watched) doesn't have the clean structure of NLP sentences. In NLP, a sentence has subjects and objects, and you can inject facts: 'Paris (City‖1⟩) is in France.' In recommendation, there's just a sequence: 'Movie A, Movie B, Movie C.' Where do you inject the new item?
1086.ap: The team adapted model editing—a technique from NLP that surgically updates facts in LLMs without retraining—to recommendation. They model the sequence context as generating semantic identifiers (short codes representing each item). To inject a new item, they (1) explicitly model how the sequence context predicts the next item's identifier, giving a structure that mirrors NLP's subject-object binding; (2) edit the model's weights at token level iteratively, injecting bundles of related item codes; (3) use a rank-one update (a lightweight matrix modification) that minimizes disruption to existing recommendations.
1086.ww: Model editing works because you're making a surgical change: 'whenever we see context pattern X, output this new item code.' By doing this at the model's weight level rather than the data level, you avoid the lag of retraining. Iterative token-level edits allow handling multi-token item bundles because you're building up the update gradually rather than trying to inject a complex pattern at once.
1086.po: The system can inject new items into a trained generative recommender without retraining, addressing the cold-start problem. Experiments show it recovers recommendation quality for new items in minutes rather than days, making it practical for real platforms.

1087.bp: Large e-commerce and social platforms like Alibaba or TikTok have both search (users type keywords) and recommendation (personalized suggestions). These are treated as separate functions, but they're connected: if you search for 'running shoes,' later recommendations should adapt. The challenge is mixing these signals effectively—search history reveals explicit intent, but not every search is useful for predicting what you'll click next.
1087.wh: Search queries are noisy: you might search for 'best pasta recipes' out of curiosity, 'laptop repair' out of frustration, or 'birthday gifts for engineers' with real intent to buy. Naive methods either ignore search history or treat all searches as equally predictive. But search behaviors frequently contain outdated or irrelevant signals—you searched for winter coats in July, and that's probably not relevant now. The system needs to *select* which search signals matter for the current recommendation task.
1087.ap: The team built a system that (1) encodes both search and recommendation histories into a unified latent representation (a compact internal code capturing your overall interests), (2) then performs iterative reasoning within that latent space to identify which search signals are most relevant to the current recommendation. The reasoning mimics how humans think: 'What does the user actually want?' and then 'Which of their past searches illuminate that intent?' They use a contrastive learning objective to guide this reasoning—making sure the selected searches align with positive recommendations and away from negative ones.
1087.ww: Working in latent space (a compressed representation) rather than raw history lets the system generalize: it learns abstract patterns of when search is useful, not memorizing specific search terms. Iterative reasoning over this space mirrors human decision-making: identify intent first, then search backward through your memory for relevant signals. The contrastive objective ensures the system isn't just picking random searches; it's selecting ones that actually predict good recommendations.
1087.po: On large-scale search-and-recommendation logs, this method beats baselines that either ignore search or use all search equally. It improves recommendation click-through rates by filtering out noisy, outdated, or irrelevant search signals while amplifying the ones that predict what users will actually engage with.

1088.bp: In online advertising, platforms decide how much to bid for ad slots and how to budget across the day. If you bid too high, you hemorrhage money; too low, your ads disappear. And the feedback you get is delayed: you place bids every minute, but advertisers see spending totals only at the end of the day. This is a control problem: you're making rapid decisions but evaluating them slowly.
1088.wh: The core mismatch is temporal granularity: decisions happen at millisecond scale (each auction), but meaningful feedback (did I spend right and get good results?) comes at the day or hour scale. This creates sparse reward signals—you make a thousand decisions before knowing if any were good. Additionally, the feedback is noisy: an ad placement's success depends on user behavior, which is chaotic. Standard reinforcement learning assumes dense, immediate rewards; here you're flying blind.
1088.ap: The team built a generative model that mirrors how humans think about this: plan at multiple time scales at once. They use a multi-scale approach that first generates day-level budget trajectories, then hour-level pacing, then individual bids. They compress the diverse feature types (bid amounts, budgets, times, campaigns) using a hierarchical quantizer (a multi-scale VQVAE—a lossy encoder that treats different types of information at appropriate resolution). The final model integrates state and action directly to capture long-term dependencies without needing auxiliary prediction networks.
1088.ww: Planning coarse-to-fine works because coarser time scales have denser, more reliable feedback: 'did we spend the budget?' is easier to evaluate than 'was this specific bid good?' By generating at multiple scales, the model can learn stable patterns at the day level, then instantiate them into fine-grained decisions. Compressing features via a hierarchical quantizer lets different types of information (continuous amounts, categorical campaigns, temporal positions) be handled naturally rather than forced into one representation.
1088.po: In both offline simulations and real advertising systems, this multi-scale generative approach outperforms standard reinforcement learning baselines. It produces more stable bids, better budget adherence, and improved return-on-ad-spend by treating the fundamental granularity mismatch explicitly.

1089.bp: When a user profile has missing information—age, location, interests—recommendation systems must guess. One approach is to copy values from the user's graph neighbors or propagate features across connections: 'this user is friends with Alice, and Alice likes jazz, so let's guess they do too.' This works okay but can overfit to the graph structure: if the graph is accidentally sparse or biased, the propagation amplifies those biases.
1089.wh: The fundamental problem is structural overfitting: diffusion-based methods assume the graph captures all relevant information, but real graphs have artifacts. Users might be disconnected not because they're genuinely unrelated but because of platform design or privacy choices. The propagation smooths features across neighbors, but it also flattens diversity—everyone ends up similar. Worst of all, when you deploy to a new platform with a different graph structure (an inductive setting), the method fails catastrophically because it learned to exploit the specific graph you trained on.
1089.ap: The team addresses this in three steps. First, they augment the graph globally: connect disjoint components to allow diffusion to flow across islands. Second, they learn a semantic manifold (an internal structure representing natural feature patterns) via masked autoencoding—like BERT, they hide features and learn to reconstruct them, capturing what realistic features look like. Third, crucially, they add a test-time correction: when deploying to a new graph, they project biased features back onto the learned manifold, correcting for structural distortions before inference.
1089.ww: Global augmentation solves the connectivity problem by bridging isolated users. The masked autoencoding learns what features should *look* like naturally, independent of graph structure—it's a kind of semantic prior. Test-time correction is the key insight: even if the new graph is different, you can rectify the distorted features by pulling them back to the learned manifold, bridging the inductive distribution gap.
1089.po: On a new real-world dataset from voyage records (Sailing), this framework mitigates all three failure modes: it maintains performance on disconnected test graphs, preserves semantic diversity without over-smoothing, and generalizes to new graph structures. The test-time rectification is particularly powerful for practical deployment.

1090.bp: When you read a news article mentioning 'the meeting on Tuesday' and later 'the decision three days after the meeting,' you need to understand that 'the decision' happened on Friday. Understanding time relationships between events is essential for machines to comprehend narratives, timelines, and causal chains.
1090.wh: The task is deceptively hard. The full temporal relation set is rich: one event can be DURING another, BEFORE, AFTER, EQUAL, OVERLAPPING, and more. But datasets and benchmarks have been progressively simplified: early work attempted all relations, but researchers found it too difficult and switched to simpler subsets, like just event-to-event relations. By narrowing scope, progress stalled—real systems need the full expressivity.
1090.ap: Instead of directly predicting complex interval relations (e.g., 'Event A overlaps Event B'), the approach decomposes the problem. It first classifies simpler point relations: the start of Event A is BEFORE the start of Event B, the end of Event A is AFTER the end of Event B, etc. Once you know the relationships between all four endpoints, you can decode these point constraints into an interval relation—e.g., if both starts are ordered and both ends are ordered in matching ways, you have DURING or OVERLAPPING.
1090.ww: Decomposing intervals into points is powerful because point relations are much simpler and more reliable to predict. A model can confidently classify 'timepoint X comes before timepoint Y' more easily than 'Event A during Event B.' By solving the simpler problem first, you avoid the combinatorial explosion of interval relations. The decoding step is deterministic: given point relationships, the interval relation follows logically.
1090.po: On the TempEval-3 benchmark, this approach achieves 70.1% temporal awareness, a new state-of-the-art. By returning to the full set of interval relations instead of simplified subsets, it enables richer temporal understanding for downstream NLP applications.

1091.bp: Dense retrievers (neural networks that embed questions and documents into similar spaces) are great at understanding meaning but sometimes rank irrelevant documents highly just because they're topically similar. Traditional sparse retrieval (BM25, keyword matching) is more conservative and less prone to false positives, but misses paraphrases and semantic variations. The ideal system would combine their strengths.
1091.wh: The problem is that failure modes are orthogonal. Dense retrievers fail by promoting 'similar-looking but irrelevant' passages; sparse retrievers fail by missing relevant passages that use different vocabulary. If you just average their scores, you're averaging across failure modes—sometimes the dense retriever is confident and wrong, sometimes the sparse retriever is confident and wrong, and you can't tell which is which.
1091.ap: The insight is elegant: relevant passages cluster in the region where *both* retrievers score highly (consensus). The team builds a re-ranker that (1) identifies anchor documents where both sparse and dense agree, (2) expands the query using these verified anchors (words and concepts from highly-agreed-upon documents), and (3) applies geometric gating to suppress drift from the original intent. The gating ensures the expanded query stays close to the original, preventing the expansion from chasing irrelevant tangents.
1091.ww: Consensus is a reliable signal: if both a lexical matcher and a semantic matcher rank a document highly, it's probably actually relevant. Expanding the query through these anchors introduces new vocabulary that both methods considered important. Geometric gating prevents the expansion from wandering—you're saying 'use these new words, but stay true to the original intent.'
1091.po: On TREC Deep Learning benchmarks, this method improves over both dense-only and sparse-only approaches by 3-5%, with a compact 33M-parameter model. Notably, these gains require no additional parameters or training beyond using retrieval signals more effectively—pure algorithmic improvement from trusting consensus.

1092.bp: Large platforms like TikTok recommend content across multiple scenarios: the homepage (general discovery), a user's following feed (accounts they track), and live streams (real-time interactions). Each scenario has different user behavior patterns—people interact differently when browsing casually versus watching a specific creator's live stream. The challenge is building a single recommender that personalizes across all these contexts.
1092.wh: Naive approaches use a shared representation for all scenarios, but this causes representation entanglement: the system can't distinguish scenario-specific signals from global ones. A better approach adds scenario-specific networks, but these don't share knowledge effectively. The real problem is distribution mismatch: user interests are expressed differently in each scenario. On the homepage, engagement might signal 'I'm browsing,' while on a live stream, it signals 'I'm focused on this creator.' Training on mixed distributions confuses the model.
1092.ap: The team builds scenario-specific prototype spaces—abstract canonical representations for each scenario. They use a multi-gate mixture of experts (a routing network that assigns items to different processing paths) to extract shared features, and independent networks for scenario-specific features. Then, they project both into their respective prototype spaces. Crucially, they use unbalanced optimal transport (a mathematical technique for matching distributions) to align distributions: it finds the best correspondence between points in each scenario's distribution, accounting for imbalances.
1092.ww: Prototype spaces are useful because they capture 'what does a good engagement look like in this scenario?' without entanglement. The multi-gate MoE efficiently routes information to the right expert. Unbalanced optimal transport is powerful because it doesn't assume scenarios have equal weight—it flexibly aligns heterogeneous distributions, solving the core problem of scenario mismatch.
1092.po: On TikTok-like multi-scenario recommendation tasks, this method improves over parameter-sharing and scenario-specific baselines by better capturing scenario-specific distributions while enabling knowledge transfer. It improves recommendation quality across all scenarios simultaneously.

1093.bp: News readers have filter bubbles: if you read a lot of U.S. politics, the recommender keeps showing you U.S. politics, never world news. This narrows your perspective and can radicalize. Platforms want to gently nudge readers toward broader coverage. But how do you diversify reading habits without making people angry by showing irrelevant articles?
1093.wh: Simple exposure diversity doesn't work: you can show diverse articles, but readers won't click if they're irrelevant. The deeper problem is that people have genuine preferences—some readers truly care less about world news than others. You can't force diversity without annoying them. And generic nudges ('try something different!') rarely work; they need to be personalized to the reader's actual interests.
1093.ap: The team ran a real field experiment with 120 news readers for five weeks using the POPROX platform. They designed two algorithmic nudges: (1) a topic-locality dual calibration that gently pushes the recommendation ranking to include both domestic and world news in proportion to the user's interest, and (2) an LLM-based presentation nudge that personalizes how each article is displayed based on the reader's prior interests—e.g., highlighting how an article relates to topics they've previously read.
1093.ww: Dual calibration works because it doesn't force diversity; it adjusts recommendations proportionally based on measured interest. If you read some world news already, show more; if you've never clicked it, nudge gently. LLM personalization works because readers engage with content better when framed in terms they understand—connecting unfamiliar topics to familiar ones increases click-through without manipulation.
1093.po: The experiment found that algorithmic nudges successfully increased diversity exposure and consumption (readers clicked more diverse articles), and longitudinal exposure shifted reading habits toward valuing balanced news from both domestic and world sources. Presentation nudges had variable effects, with relevance-based framing outperforming generic personalization.

1094.bp: Current recommenders learn from thousands of interactions—clicks, ratings, purchases—specific to each user. But what if you had a model that could recommend from just a few examples, like a human expert who can infer preferences instantly? Such a system could work with new users without waiting for data, and generalize across different platforms and item catalogs.
1094.wh: Most recommenders are dataset-specific: train on Netflix, works on Netflix; train on Amazon, works on Amazon. They need weeks of interaction data per user. The reason is that they learn specific patterns for each domain. What's missing is a *general* ability to infer preferences from small numbers of examples—the kind of generalization humans have. Scaling up recommenders with more data helps marginally, but it doesn't solve the fundamental problem of domain transfer.
1094.ap: The team created a 'prior-fitted network' trained entirely on synthetic data—simulated clickstreams generated from a structural causal model (a generative model that mimics how user preferences and item features interact). The real innovation: pretraining on this synthetic diversity acts like a Bayesian prior, teaching the model to perform amortized inference. At test time, you give it a few real interactions, and a simple transformer conditions on them to make predictions—no weight updates, just a forward pass.
1094.ww: Training on synthetic data with diverse causal structure teaches the model invariant principles: 'how do preferences manifest across different user types and item catalogs?' Because the training distribution is broad and structured, the model learns to generalize. Amortized inference means the model has learned a kind of Bayesian reasoning: given a small support set of observations, compute the posterior distribution over preferences, then use it to predict.
1094.po: Across eight public benchmarks, RecPFN achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance (no fine-tuning on target domain) while remaining competitive with fully supervised methods in low-data regimes. It's deployment-efficient, robust to domain shift, and offers a practical path to data-efficient, generalizable recommenders.
